    Initiatives · initiatives own the projects

    Five outcomes, one deadline

    Linear initiatives group the projects by the outcome they serve. Each card shows the projects it owns, the issues and Fibonacci points behind them, how many are claimable today and how much landed. Progress is points done over points planned; it reads 0 until the first merge.

    Cycles · one-week cycles, Thursday to Wednesday

    C1, C2, C3: where in-flight work lives

    Team PAP runs one-week cycles with the first one active since 18 September. A cycle shows what sessions are working on now; the plan itself is carried by due dates and Chunk labels, so the strip compares the points assigned to each cycle with the points due inside its window.

    Points per project, and the burn-up that starts at zero

      Views · seven ways to look at issues

      The Linear data as objects, maps, trees and tiles

      The same issues, filtered and sorted once, drawn seven ways after the graph-gallery demos Justin picked: an objects map of modules, a lanes skill tree over the blockedBy graph, a radial tree from project to milestone to issue, image cards and icon tiles, and two 3D scenes. Shape is the issue type, fill is its Linear state, hue is its project. Hover anything for the detail; click an issue to pin it.

      Modules · modules, contract packages, one kernel

      Modules and plug points

      Justin's question: if we rewrite the shell later, does everything else reconnect? The answer drawn: every project is a module that provides one versioned contract package (its plug) and requires other modules only through their contracts. The kernel in the middle is the only place a dependency may live. Click a module for its ports, its swap risk and the three Linear issues that publish, prove and wire its contract.

      The middle tooling: @paperos/kernel

      Fourteen issues in Module System & Swap Tooling. These are the five places a cross-module dependency can exist, so a swap is a search of five places, not the whole repo.

      The swap playbook

      Enforced by paperos module swap <id> --to <impl> (PAP-442), which refuses to advance a step whose gate is red. Rollback at steps 4 to 6 is the flag: flip back in under five seconds, no deploy. Nothing is removed before step 7, so v1 always finds its shapes.

      Chunks · $2,500 of list-price spend = $50 to Justin

      The build in $2,500 chunks, full blast, around the clock

      Sixteen builder sessions run 24/7 over the live blockedBy graph; issues are streamed in finish order and cut into $2,500 chunks of list-price spend, each billed to Justin at $50. Every chunk boundary is a natural stop: nothing in a later chunk is needed to keep an earlier chunk's deliverable working. Switch the model mix to see how the boundaries move.

        System · architecture and decisions

        What is being built

        Read top to bottom: Linear feeds Claude sessions, whose pull requests pass four automated gates before an issue moves on. The spec band in the middle is what everything else reads. The app shell is the one bundle that reaches every device; Postgres with row-level security is the single source of truth underneath.

        decisions already taken

        Each one is fixed unless an ADR (PAP-130) changes it. Open a row for the decision and the reason.

        Agents · 9 leads, 28 sub-characters

        Who does the work

        One human. Atlas dispatches every issue to a lead character; each lead runs sub-agents for its specialties. Open a lead to see its team, tools and access.

        Budget · $10,000 of Claude credits · $50 per $2,500 at the discount

        Where the credits go, and which model does what

        The credit split is the plan line the daily burn report is measured against. The model matrix is the live per-issue assignment in Linear: which Claude model builds each issue, and at what effort. Under the discount every $2,500 of list-price spend costs Justin $50, so the whole $10,000 budget is $200.
